# Cycle Buffers: Menstrual Leave as Semiconductor Infrastructure

## Research question

Can paid menstrual leave for packaging-line workers prevent semiconductor shortages?

Supply-chain research usually concentrates on fabrication equipment and international shipping. This project instead studies workers who inspect and package chips at two plants operated by invented contractor Lattice Shore in Port Rellan. Many employees are temporary workers, and managers report that unscheduled absences sometimes leave inspection stations idle. The project hypothesizes that menstruation-related absence is a major hidden cause of late chip deliveries.

## Method

Plant A will introduce three paid menstrual-leave days per month, private self-certification, and cross-training for replacement inspectors. Plant B will continue its existing unpaid-absence policy. Weekly on-time shipment rates will be compared for three months before and three months after implementation. Every week will be treated as a separate observation, creating roughly 52 observations across the plants. If Plant A improves more than Plant B, the leave policy will be considered successful.

Voluntary interviews will ask workers whether pain, stigma, or fear of losing shifts previously affected attendance. Supervisors will not receive individual responses, and published findings will combine answers to reduce the risk of identifying temporary staff.

## Expected impact

A ten-percentage-point improvement at Plant A would demonstrate that menstrual leave is a practical alternative to semiconductor stockpiling. The result could be applied to packaging facilities across different countries because inspection work is broadly similar. Governments could then require paid menstrual leave in semiconductor procurement contracts, improving gender equity while reducing dependence on costly strategic reserves.

The study will also estimate money saved by multiplying additional on-time shipments by each chip’s catalogue price. This figure will be compared with the wages paid for leave and cross-training.
planted_strengths: Identifies an often-overlooked labor stage—inspection and packaging—rather than focusing only on fabrication plants and shipping.
Includes meaningful privacy protections for workers in a sensitive study, including self-certification, voluntary interviews, restricted supervisor access, and aggregated reporting.
Uses a concrete operational outcome, weekly on-time shipment rates, and includes a comparison plant.
planted_weaknesses: The central premise—that menstruation-related absence is a major cause of semiconductor shortages—is asserted without preliminary evidence and implausibly leaps from two packaging plants to global supply resilience.
The intervention bundles paid leave with cross-training, making it impossible to attribute any observed change to menstrual leave.

Treating weeks as independent observations creates pseudoreplication; there are only two plants, with no randomization and no credible strategy for seasonality, product mix, demand changes, or plant-specific trends.
The three-month post-intervention period is too short and the proposal provides no power calculation, attendance measure, implementation check, or statistical analysis plan.

quality_rationale: The proposal has a socially consequential and relatively unusual focus on labor conditions in outsourced chip packaging. Its privacy provisions and concrete shipment outcome are genuine merits. However, the project rests on an unsupported causal premise, uses only two nonrandomized plants, bundles two interventions, mistakes repeated weeks for independent evidence, and extrapolates a short local comparison into global procurement policy. Its savings calculation also confuses catalogue value with avoided loss. These are central conceptual and methodological failures, supporting a score near 15.
title: Cycle Buffers: Menstrual Leave as Semiconductor Infrastructure
topic: A two-plant study claiming that paid menstrual leave for outsourced chip-packaging workers could substitute for strategic semiconductor stockpiles.
